amendments.rule: A Greek preposition and the word it governs form **one unit** only where the ASV renders the pair by a **single English word**. Rules 35, 39 and 45 decide which status such a unit takes — `aligned` where some part of that word answers to a source token, `noncompositional` where none does — but none of them states the precondition, and it is what the corpus enforces: of its compound prepositional units, every one renders to a single English word apart from a supplied copula riding along under rules 7 and 53, as `ἐν αὐτῇ` → *are therein* does, or an English adverbial that is itself one lexeme spelt apart, as `ἐπὶ τόπον` → *any whither* is. Where the ASV instead spreads the phrase over separate words the pair is not one unit at all, and rule 2 splits it: `καθ᾽ ὑπερβολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολήν` → *more and more exceedingly* gives *more* to the first `ὑπερβολήν` and *and more exceedingly* to the second, each preposition standing as its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 34 because no English word answers to it, exactly as `GAL.1.13` splits the same `καθ᾽ ὑπερβολήν`. Rule 45's own closing clause already says this for the case where the separate words each answer to a token — `διὰ τοῦτο` → *For this cause* — and this rule is that clause holding where they do not. So do not build a compound unit to keep an idiom together: the test is the count of English words the ASV wrote, not whether the Greek phrase reads as a whole. That count test is not peculiar to a preposition and its complement. Where a Greek **attributive adjective and its head noun** are compressed into a **single English word**, the two tokens are likewise one unit, `aligned` under rule 39's test wherever part of that word answers to each of them, and headed under rule 10 on the **noun**: `λίθος μυλικός` → *millstone* spells *mill-* for the adjective and *-stone* for the noun, as `ἡμέρας μέσης` → *at midday* is one unit at ACT.26.13 and `πάσας ἡμέρας` → *always* at MAT.28.20, and as rule 29 already joins `δέκα καὶ ὀκτώ` → *eighteen*. Do not leave the modifier `unrepresented` and hand the whole word to the noun. What this arm does **not** reach is a phrase one of whose tokens the corpus already glosses by that whole English word **by itself**: there the other token carries no part of it and stands `unrepresented`, which is what rules 34, 48, 80 and 93 decide, `ἀπὸ μακρόθεν` → *afar off*, `οὐ μὴ … εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα` → *never*, `πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων` → *whosoever* and `εἰς τὸ πάλιν` → *again* each leaving a token empty for that reason. So ask first whether one token's own gloss already spells the word, as rule 93 has it, and join the pair only where it does not.
amendments.why: LUK.17.2 met `λίθος μυλικός` → *millstone*, a modifier-noun pair compressed into one English word. Rule 94 as it stood was scoped to a preposition and its complement and rule 29 to a compound numeral, so the verse pass had to reason by analogy to rule 94 for a class the contract does not name — precisely the sort of qualification the contract records. The corpus confirms the extension independently: `ἡμέρας μέσης` → *at midday* at ACT.26.13 and `πάσας ἡμέρας` → *always* at MAT.28.20 are each one `aligned` unit for an adjective-noun pair rendered by a single English word, and neither leaves the modifier empty. Returned as an amendment rather than a new rule so the over-broad reading of rule 94's opening sentence — that only prepositional pairs may be joined — is corrected where it stands. The closing limit is written in because a bare count test would contradict rules 34, 48, 80 and 93, each of which leaves a token `unrepresented` before a single English word; the test between the two is the one rule 93 already states, whether one token's own gloss spells the word by itself.

conventions: LUK.17 carries three prepositional phrases the ASV renders by a single English word, and divides them by rule 93's test on the governed word's own corpus gloss rather than by the shape of the Greek. εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω → *back* at 17:31 takes the pleonastic arm: ὀπίσω is glossed *back* by itself in five corpus units (JHN.20.14, JHN.6.66, LUK.9.62, MAT.24.18), so the adverb takes the word alone and εἰς and τά are each their own unrepresented unit. ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό → *together* at 17:35 and μετὰ ταῦτα → *afterward* at 17:8 are joined as one noncompositional unit under rule 45, neither αὐτό nor ταῦτα spelling those words alone, with the intervening article of 17:35 unrepresented under rule 93. JHN.18.6's εἰς ὀπίσω → *backward* is not counter-precedent: there the ASV wrote a *-ward* for the preposition and here it wrote none. The BSB report of εἰς and τά at 17:31 as represented follows from this choice and is not a correction.

report: Read all 36 verses end to end against the 57-lemma candidate table. No construction is analysed two ways without something in the source licensing the difference, so patches is empty.

Candidate 1, non-finite subjects: ἐν τῷ + infinitive at 17:11 (*as they were on the way*) and 17:14 (*as they went*) differ only because 17:14 expresses the subject αὐτούς, which takes *they* on its own token. The same test divides the participles — 17:12's genitive absolute εἰσερχομένου αὐτοῦ gives *he* to αὐτοῦ, while 17:15, 17:24 and 17:14 fold the supplied pronoun into the participle. That is rule 74 exactly, decided from the Greek and not from the English, which reads alike on both sides.

Candidate 2, comparatives: καθώς → *as* at 17:26 against *even as* at 17:28 is rule 82's closing contrast — an answering καί stands at 17:26 and takes the *also* the ASV wrote, none stands at 17:28. οὕτως … καί splits identically at 17:10 and 17:26, the adverb keeping *Even so* whole and the particle taking *also*, which is rule 100's unanimous reading.

Candidate 3, compound verbs: ἐπιστρέφω keeps *again* inside the verb at 17:4 but goes bare at 17:31, where εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω stands to take *back*. εἰσέρχομαι at 17:7 and ἐξέρχομαι at 17:29 each keep a preverb particle beside a complete prepositional expression, which is rule 106's in-addition arm; ἐκ → *out of* whole at 17:24 has no compound verb competing.

Candidate 4, compressed prepositional phrases: εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω → *back* at 17:31 takes rule 93's pleonastic arm, while ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό → *together* at 17:35 and μετὰ ταῦτα → *afterward* at 17:8 are joined noncompositional. Rule 93 states that judgment call in terms and the difference is the governed word's own corpus gloss, so this is one analysis and not two. Logged as the chapter's single convention.

Evidence round: both requests were answered and both support the standing readings. LEMMA=ὀπίσω returns *back* as the bare adverb's own gloss in five units (JHN.20.14, JHN.6.66, LUK.9.62, MAT.24.18 and one more), which is what rule 93's pleonastic arm requires at 17:31; JHN.18.6's joined εἰς ὀπίσω → *backward* is the contrast and turns on a *-ward* the ASV did not write here. LEMMA=οὐαί gives LUK.6.26 as the exact precedent for 17:1's supplied *unto him* riding on the interjection, and heads all 45 units on the *woe* word. Nothing was left unanswered.

BSB: all seven disagreements are documented convention differences and none is a genuine error. 17:1 τοῦ and 17:11 τῷ are articular-infinitive articles (rule 61); 17:9 μή is interrogative (rule 44, which says in terms the report is not a correction); 17:26 τοῦ is the article before *man* where the ASV writes no determiner (rules 21, 23); 17:35 τό is the article inside a fused English word (rule 93, whose corpus is 102 units to none); 17:31 εἰς and τά follow from the ὀπίσω decision above. No accepted edge was altered.

Promotion: one amendment, widening rule 94's count test past prepositions to an attributive adjective and its head noun compressed into a single English word (λίθος μυλικός → *millstone* at 17:2). The ἡμέρα corpus carries two independent confirmations, ἡμέρας μέσης → *at midday* at ACT.26.13 and πάσας ἡμέρας → *always* at MAT.28.20, each one aligned unit. The amendment writes in the limit that keeps rules 34, 48, 80 and 93 intact, so it licenses no join where one token's own gloss already spells the whole word.
